analysis.one_liner: Extends Social Security payroll taxes up to $400,000 of income and raises investment taxes on top earners.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2025 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no further action; it has no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make high earners keep paying Social Security payroll taxes on wages between today's annual cap (about $176,000 in 2025) and $400,000. It would add a 1.2% Medicare tax on wages and self-employment income above $400,000 ($500,000 for couples), and would roughly quadruple the tax on investment income for people making more than $400,000 and for trusts and estates. All of the new revenue would flow into the Social Security and Medicare trust funds.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security and Medicare beneficiaries, whose trust funds receive the new revenue and whose benefits are the reason the bill exists.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would apply the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax to wages between the annual contribution and benefit base and $400,000, so high earners pay into the program on more of their income [S2].
It would add a 1.2% Medicare tax on wages and self-employment income above $400,000 for single filers and $500,000 for joint filers [S2].
It would raise the tax on net investment income for individuals above the $400,000/$500,000 threshold by an additional 13.6%, and raise the rate for trusts and estates from 3.8% to 17.4% [S2].
All new revenue would be deposited into the trust funds: 71.3% to the old-age and survivors fund, 10.3% to disability, and 28.7% to the Medicare hospital insurance fund [S2].

analysis.who_pays: People earning above roughly $400,000 a year, self-employed professionals above that threshold, trusts and estates, and investors with large investment incomes.

drawbacks.text: Self-employed people whose income falls between the current wage cap and $400,000 would face a new tax they do not pay today, since the bill applies Social Security tax to that band of earnings [S2].
The bill raises the trust-fund tax rate for trusts and estates to 17.4%, more than four times the current 3.8%, a sharply higher rate on inherited and estate-held investment income [S2].

The tax structure is complex: the wage-band tax applies only in years when the wage base is under $400,000, and the investment-income increase is phased in over a $100,000 band, which adds compliance burden and planning opportunities [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would meaningfully slow the depletion of the Social Security and Medicare trust funds by taxing high earners and investment income, which currently stop contributing payroll tax above the wage cap. The cost falls entirely on households above roughly $400,000 a year and on trusts, which can bear it; the main honest objections are the added complexity and the hit to high-earning self-employed professionals in the newly taxed wage band.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 8, 2025 by Rep. Brendan Boyle of Pennsylvania [S1].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S4].
No member of the House has cosponsored the bill [S3].
The full action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote after the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost a vote on the bill; high earners and large investors are better off in the meantime because the current payroll tax cap and the 3.8% investment-income rate remain in place.

for.name: Rep. Brendan F. Boyle
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means.

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled any hearing, markup, or vote on the bill since it was referred to the committee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member of either party cosponsored it, so the partisan split never formed on the record; the sponsor is a Democrat and the committee chair who has not acted is a Republican.

industries.note: They would pay Social Security tax on a new band of wages and an added 1.2% Medicare tax; the status quo lets wages above the cap go untaxed for Social Security. Their interest in avoiding the tax runs against the trust funds ordinary beneficiaries rely on.

industries.industry: Investment funds and large investors (private equity, hedge funds, trusts and estates)
industries.note: The bill roughly quadruples the investment-income tax rate for trusts and estates and adds a 13.6% surtax on high earners' investment income. These taxes directly fund the Social Security and Medicare benefits the bill is designed to protect.

Doctors, lawyers, and other partners with income between the current wage cap and $400,000 would face Social Security self-employment tax they do not owe today. Their interest in avoiding it runs against shoring up the programs their clients depend on.

analysis.trajectory: With no cosponsors and no committee action nearly a year into the session, the bill is on the standard path of a minority-party tax bill: it will likely die in the Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or vote unless its sponsor builds a cosponsor list or a future Congress picks it up.
